fixes.explanation: Scattered does show up earlier, when David asks the LORD to "scatter them." (Psalm 144:6) But that's a different moment in the psalm. For his closing, David says, "Blessed are the people of whom this is so; blessed are the people whose God is the LORD." (Psalm 144:15) That's the word he lands on for them, and it isn't scattered.

Nice, careful hands do come to mind, and I respect a good stitch. But David says the LORD trains his hands "for war" and his fingers "for battle." (Psalm 144:1) No needles in this verse, friend. This is David talking about the fight, and about who trained him for it.

That's it. David says the LORD is "…my shield, in whom I take refuge…" (Psalm 144:2) Taking refuge means running TO something safe. When a blazing hot tray comes out of my oven, I dive behind the cooling rack, but David picked a much better place to hide.

You got it. David asks, "O LORD, what is man, that You regard him, the son of man that You think of him?" (Psalm 144:3) I think he's amazed that the LORD thinks of us at all. I think that's a good place to land after all that talk of fortresses.

That's a thoughtful guess, and it's close to the neighborhood. But David asks why the LORD "regards" man and "thinks of" him. (Psalm 144:3) He isn't asking why people were made. I think he's amazed that the LORD pays attention to us at all.

I see where that came from, since this psalm has some big, stormy asks coming. But in verse 3, David asks, "…what is man, that You regard him, the son of man that You think of him?" (Psalm 144:3) Nothing about a judging day there. I think it's wonder, plain and simple.

Right. David asks, "Flash forth Your lightning and scatter them; shoot Your arrows and rout them." (Psalm 144:6) To rout someone means to beat them so they run. David is asking the LORD for a full win.

That's a kind thought, baker, and I like the heart behind it. But the verse says "scatter them" and "rout them." (Psalm 144:6) Arrows aren't how you lead anybody to safety. David is asking for them to be scattered and routed.

That's the one. David says, "I will sing to You a new song, O God; on a harp of ten strings I will make music to You…" (Psalm 144:9) He's in the middle of asking for rescue, and he says he will sing. That's a lot of music promised in the middle of a prayer.

True. David sings to "…Him who gives victory to kings, who frees His servant David from the deadly sword." (Psalm 144:10) Notice he calls himself His servant. The song goes to the One who gives the victory and frees him from the sword.
Good guess, but servants aren't in this verse. David says, "…our sons will be like plants nurtured in their youth…" (Psalm 144:12) It's the sons who get the plant picture, nurtured in their youth.
Right. David says, "…our daughters like corner pillars carved to adorn a palace." (Psalm 144:12) To adorn means to decorate. So these pillars are carved to make a palace beautiful.
Yes. David says, "There will be no breach in the walls…" (Psalm 144:14) A breach is a break in a wall. In his picture, the walls have none.
Not quite, friend. David's picture says the opposite. He says there will be "…no going into captivity…" (Psalm 144:14) So no captivity is part of what he pictures.

Correct, it's false. David says there will be "…no breach in the walls, no going into captivity, and no cry of lament in our streets." (Psalm 144:14) The statement says the opposite of what David says. In his picture, there's no going into captivity.

I know it's a tempting word, but it doesn't fit this ending. David says, "Blessed are the people of whom this is so; blessed are the people whose God is the LORD." (Psalm 144:15) Forgotten is a word I know well from my years in the back of a junk drawer, but it isn't David's closing word. He calls them blessed, twice.
